english_translation: Our ancestors used bows and arrows when they went hunting in the forest.

dialogue.shona: Madzitateguru edu aishandisa uta nemiseve kana vachienda kunovhima musango.
dialogue.english: Our ancestors used bows and arrows when they went hunting in the forest.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Madzitateguru [plural dzitateguru] • edu [edu] • aishandisa [aishandisa] • uta [uta] • nemiseve [and / with miseve] • kana [if / when / or] • vachienda [people chienda] • kunovhima [to / at novhima] • musango [in / singular sango]

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('kunovhima')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'kunovhima' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nemiseve'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nemiseve'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'miseve' forms 'nemiseve'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

cultural_notes.title: Traditional Woodland Hunting ('Kuvhima muSango') & Conservation Rules
cultural_notes.content: Historically, skilled hunters ('vavhimi') ventured into the forest ('musango') with bows and arrows ('uta nemiseve'), guided by strict customary ecological rules ('zviera') that forbade hunting sacred species or breeding animals.

active_exercises.prompt: You want to politely ask an elder or a group of guests to sit down ('gara'). Which imperative form should you use?
active_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' to the verb stem ('gara' -> 'garai') forms the plural and polite command in Shona.

active_exercises.explanation: 'Manheru' is the greeting used in the evening, paired with 'makadini henyu?' ('how are you?').
